She would live among people who loved her and had better judgment than she did, with enough seclusion to keep her safe and enough to do to keep her cheerful. She would neither be led into temptation nor left alone for it to find her. She would be respected and happy; and Emma acknowledged that she was the luckiest person in the world to have inspired such steadfast, enduring love in such a man—or, if not quite the luckiest, second only to herself.

Harriet's commitments to the Martins naturally took her away, and she spent less and less time at Hartfield. This was no cause for regret. The closeness between her and Emma had to diminish; their friendship had to settle into a quieter kind of affection. Fortunately, what ought to happen, and had to happen, already seemed to be beginning in the most gradual and natural way.

Before September ended, Emma accompanied Harriet to church and watched her marry Robert Martin with a satisfaction so complete that no memories, even those associated with Mr. Elton standing before them, could spoil it. Perhaps, indeed, she hardly saw Mr. Elton then except as the clergyman whose next blessing at the altar might be for her. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last of the three couples to become engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The two Mr. Churchills were also in London; they were waiting only for November.

The month between was the one Emma and Mr. Knightley had chosen, as firmly as they dared. They had decided that they should marry while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, allowing them to spend a fortnight away on the seaside trip they had planned. John and Isabella, and every other friend, approved. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could they persuade Mr. Woodhouse to agree? He had never yet spoken of their marriage except as something far in the future.

When they first raised the subject, he was so distressed that they almost lost hope. A second mention, however, caused him less pain. He began to think it would happen, and that he could not prevent it—a very promising stage on the mind's journey toward acceptance. Still, he was not happy. Indeed, he seemed so far from happy that his daughter's courage failed her. She could not bear to see him suffer, knowing that he imagined himself neglected. Although her reason almost accepted the assurances of both Mr. Knightleys that, once the wedding was over, his distress would soon pass too, she hesitated. She could not go ahead.

Spirits of the storm, receive me! Powers of destruction, open your arms and hold me forever! Unless a kinder power has chosen another end, so that after long suffering I may receive my reward and feel my heart beating close to another heart like mine again.

The Tiber, a road laid by nature's own hand through her continent, lay at my feet, and many boats were tied along its banks. With a few books, some provisions, and my dog, I would take one of them and drift down the river to the sea. Then, staying close to land, I would follow the beautiful shores and sunny headlands of the blue Mediterranean, pass Naples and travel along Calabria, and brave the twin dangers of Scylla and Charybdis. Fearlessly—for what had I to lose?—I would cross the sea toward Malta and the more distant Cyclades. I would avoid Constantinople: its familiar towers and inlets belonged to a life utterly different from mine now. I would follow Asia Minor and Syria, pass the Nile's seven mouths, and turn north again. Leaving forgotten Carthage and deserted Libya behind, I would reach the pillars of Hercules. And then—wherever I might go—the muddy caves and silent depths of the sea might become my home before this long voyage ended. Disease might strike my heart as I drifted alone on the restless Mediterranean. Or, somewhere I landed, I might find what I sought—a companion. If that could not be, the solitary wanderer would keep raising his sail and gripping the tiller forever, frail and grey-haired, his youth already buried with those he loved. Still following heaven's breezes, he would round one headland after another, anchor in bay after bay, and cross the barren ocean. Leaving the green land of his native Europe behind, I might sail down Africa's tawny coast, survive the Cape's fierce seas, and moor my battered little boat in a creek shaded by fragrant spice groves on distant islands of the Indian Ocean.

These are wild dreams. Yet they have ruled my imagination ever since they came to me a week ago, as I stood high on St. Peter's. I have chosen my boat and put my few supplies aboard. I have selected a handful of books, chiefly Homer and Shakespeare. But the world's libraries stand open to me, and I can replenish my collection in any port. I do not expect any change for the better; yet I cannot endure the sameness of the present.

My father had been the life of my life, and his memory was so still. I could feel gratitude toward someone else, but I could never again love or hope as I once had. Everything was suffering; even my pleasures were endured, not enjoyed. I was like a lonely place among mountains, enclosed on every side by steep black cliffs, where no warmth could enter and no path led out to sunnier fields. So, although friendship soothed me for a time, it could not restore me. It came like a gentle visitor; it left, and I scarcely felt its loss. The will to live was dead within me. Do not be surprised, then, that I welcomed heaven's best gift—a friend—with so little joy, or mourned its departure with so little bitterness.

My friend's name was Woodville. I will briefly tell his story, so that you may judge how cold my heart must have been to resist his eloquent words and tender sympathy. You will also see how, since he too was deeply unhappy, we might have comforted each other, had misery not turned me to stone like the head of Medusa. Woodville's troubles did not strike at the heart's deepest core as mine did. His grief was natural, capable of purifying the heart rather than destroying it. When its shadow passed, he might emerge brighter and happier than before.

Woodville was the son of a poor clergyman and had been educated in the classics. He was among those very few people whom fortune favours from birth, showering them without limit with gifts of mind and body. Under her special protection, no imperfection, however slight, and no disappointment, however brief, seemed permitted to touch him. She appeared to have made his mind from excellence that nothing base could stain, and given him an understanding that no error could lead astray. His genius was extraordinary; when it rose like a bright star in the east, everyone turned toward it in admiration. He was a poet. That name has been cheapened so often that it cannot convey everything he was. He resembled an ancient poet whom the Muses had crowned in his cradle and whose lips had nourished bees. As he walked among other men, a heavenly glow seemed to surround him, setting him apart and raising him above them. His exceptional beauty, the dazzling fire in his eyes, and the rich sound of his words, which left listeners silent with delighted wonder, made him tower above everyone else. In his presence, they seemed to have been created only to serve his greater excellence.
